title: Four Foundations of Mindfulness, Part 0: Introduction
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating loving-kindness towards others by recognizing that our minds are capable of both love and hatred, but also that we can learn to manage these impulses through awareness and practice. By becoming more aware of our thoughts and emotions, we can avoid getting caught up in negative patterns and instead cultivate a more compassionate and inclusive world. This requires a willingness to let go of preconceptions and be open-minded, allowing us to see others as complex individuals with their own unique qualities.

So what popped into my mind was the teaching of the four foundations of mindfulness, the teaching of the four foundations of mindfulness, as a way to practice sort of attuning ourselves, opening up our inner antennae, getting interested in a grounded way in these processes of mind, and feeling, and feeling what happens for us.

So for the main text, and there's no reason you have to get the book unless you have read all the books that you have on yourselves already.

So first the title.
The title of the Sutra in the Pali language, which is a language of South India that became the canonical language of early Buddhism.
It was not in fact the language Buddha taught.
Buddha didn't speak this language, so if somebody tells you that, they're kind of simplifying.
So the title they gave it is Satipatthana.
Sati is the word that gets translated as mindfulness, which of course is a big movement, and it's how I make my living.
So I'm interested in that word.
The original word meant something like to remember, to recollect, to bear in mind.
And it was used in the pre-Buddhist Vedic tradition to signify remembering the sacred texts.
So it already had a religious kind of cast to it.
And so some English scholar had to figure out what English word to apply to that.
There's not exactly an English word for that.
So they chose the word mindfulness, bearing something in mind, holding something in mind.
Which is pretty good, pretty close.
And Sati is also a mental factor and part of a complex sort of system in Buddhist psychology of looking at how consciousness works.
It's primarily the quality of mind that helps you bring your attention back, back to what you're intending to hold your attention on.
Then it cooperates with other factors, concentration, attention, understanding, and so on.
So this has to do with mindfulness.
It has to do with remembering something deep that we maybe forget, that we need to remember, and to come back to, to come back to.
So it's remembering, it's coming back.
The second part, Patana, Sati Patana, turns out there's two different ways that you can make sense of that term.
One way is that it means a place or a presence or an arousing.
So it's a place where you can practice mindfulness, a sort of arousing of mindfulness, a sort of area or focus for mindfulness.
I suppose these two meanings are pretty close.
The other meaning is setting forth or putting something forward, like a starting point or an origin, a beginning point.

So it's a place to start or a place to be in mindfulness.
It's translated in different ways.

That gets added in English because there's four of them.
But sometimes it gets translated as the four establishments of mindfulness, the four foundations of mindfulness, sometimes the four roots of mindfulness, Thich Nhat Hanh's establishments.
So there's going to be four major topics that we're going to look at with mindfulness.
Let's set the scene and read the first section.
This is a very famous early Buddhist teaching.
*I heard these words of the Buddha one time when he was living in Kamasamadama, a market town of the Kuru people.

It was originally just recited orally.
There are also versions of this written in Sanskrit, which has largely been lost.

Since we're trying to understand the inner workings of our minds and hearts, the Buddhists invented words and used common words in particular ways.
So every time it gets translated, the translators have to figure out what they're really trying to say, what the essence of it is.
The section in here, the very enthusiastic section where the Buddha says "because there is a most wonderful way," turns out to be Thich Nhat Hanh's translation of a Pali term, ekayana, ekayana maga.
Maga is path, so he didn't use the word path.
And ekayana, which he translated as most wonderful, actually doesn't mean most wonderful.
It turns out it means one directional, one way.
That's interesting.
So the suggestion is that if you practice in this way, you won't revert.
You won't go back.
You'll make progress that's irreversible.
This is a big statement.
He's saying here, whichever way we slice the language, that these teachings are a big deal, and it's going to really help us.
Then he asks a rhetorical question: what are these four establishments, four foundations?
He answers his own question.
First one.

Diligent, with clear understanding, mindful, having abandoned every craving and every distaste for this life.*
That's the first one.
There's a formula here that's going to be repeated.
Two.

Diligent, with clear understanding, mindful, having abandoned every craving and every distaste for this life.*
Three.
*He remains established in the observation of the mind in the mind.
Diligent, with clear understanding, mindful, having abandoned every craving and every distaste for this life.*
Four.
*He remains established in the observation of the objects of mind in the objects of mind.
Diligent, with clear understanding, mindful, having abandoned every craving and every distaste for this life.*
You notice that every word but one in those four paragraphs was repeated, which is common in these texts.
You have to merge with a certain style of speaking and listening.
In this material it's hard.
You can't just read it or listen to it like a storybook or a novel.
It's a different kind of writing and speaking and listening.
So the foundations of mindfulness are the body, first one.
Next, feelings.
The feelings is a root feeling of feelings, not like emotions so much.
The feeling, the feeling of a moment, the deep feeling.
Body, feelings.
Then the mind: the thoughts and emotions, the objects that arise in the mind, which we get so entranced by, spend 99% of our lives in.
People sit down to meditate for the first time and they're maybe a little horrified.
And then they say to you [unclear: "a letter"], "Oh, I can't meditate.

I can't meditate.
I could not quiet my mind."
And you say, "Oh, sorry to tell you, this is not about that."
And then the fourth is the most difficult to translate.
Thich Nhat Hanh translates the fourth foundation, which in the original is dharmas, as observation of the objects of mind.
I prefer patterns.
Patterns of mind.
Or just patterns.
The big patterns of our lives.
So that's the beginning of the text, and he's going to go on to give us some practices.
It will be really interesting to slowly unpack that repeated formula.

He's saying there's a particular way to do this, a particular way to be mindful and curious about the body, about these basis of feeling, about the objects in the mind, about the big patterns in the mind.
It sounds like a little bit of work.
It's diligent.
Mindful.
And there may be some conditions that facilitate that.

There's the line at the end about working with our desires and our aversions, our cravings, which, as we were saying a little bit earlier, are part of what blinds us to the sprouting seeds that lead to racism.

Thich Nhat Hanh wrote it as that you should have abandoned craving and distaste in this life.
Abandoned craving and distaste, which is itself the whole thing.
Anyway, we'll see how that goes, and whether it's helpful.
